utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Mr. Ivetic, yesterday we instructed you to upload into e-court the document that also has the number IC189. In the circumstances where there is no B/C/S version of that document, it's unnecessary, I think, for it to be uploaded into e-court and it's sufficient that it has an IC number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Ognjenovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The cross-examination by Mr. Stamp will continue in a moment. Please remember that the solemn declaration to speak the truth which you made at the outset of your evidence continues to apply to that evidence today. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Under the then-existing law, the law on personal identification cards in Serbia at the time, persons above the age of 14 years old were obliged to have in their possession an identification card; that's your understanding?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, I believe it was after 16 years of age that it was obligatory, but you could get it earlier if you wanted it. I'm not quite sure, but I think that's the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. I think if maybe I could remind you of until the 31st of April it was 16 years old and then thereafter the president, Mr. Milutinovic, passed a decree lowering the age to 14. Is that your memory?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. And wasn't that law to be strictly adhered to, at least enforced, particularly in Kosovo and Metohija because of the conditions there?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. We enforced it. I just can't remember it exactly at this moment, but I'm sure we did it. I can't remember the age limit precisely at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: With respect to this line of questioning, I think it needs to be taken into account that the witness testified that documents are issued by the SUPs and that he actually was a member of the border police and not the entity that would have been issuing ID cards. So I think that Mr. Stamp is really asking for speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Two things I think in response to that, Mr. Ivetic. One is that it can be covered in re-examination; and secondly, it's not self-evident that the proposition you've stated is right, that the witness would have absolutely no involvement in this matter, bearing in mind the significance of proof of identity to cross a border in normal circumstances. So please continue, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When on the 27th these persons showed up without ID cards, did they not tell you, all of them tell you, that their ID cards had been seized by the Prizren police?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said these people came to the border crossing. I didn't ask for their IDs, because an ID is not a document that enables you to cross a border. I asked for a passport from people over age. There were many women and children and there were very few men over 18. I talked to them and they told me that their documents were held from them at SUP Prizren. It was my -- not my duty to ask them for IDs. I was interested in seeing whether they had valid travel documents, whether they meet the requirements for crossing the state border or not. After that I checked with the SUP Prizren and they said that none of their documents were being held there, which means they probably deceived me by saying that their documents were being held there. But maybe that's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When did you check with SUP Prizren?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After they left. I again checked whether any IDs were held at the duty service of SUP Prizren and I got a negative answer, that nobody's documents were held there. Because at that time there were no column of refugees, those were among the first persons who came to the border crossing intending to leave Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: But you are now telling me now that you checked whether the IDs were held at the duty service at SUP Prizren? I thought that you were not interested in IDs, you were interested in travel documents.

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't checking IDs. I just asked if any personal documents were held at SUP Prizren. I didn't ask specifically about IDs or travel documents. I asked in general whether any personal documents were held by SUP Prizren for their territory. I didn't ask specifically for IDs or travel documents. I just asked if any personal documents were being held there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You have said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's not clear who that answer refers to. Who did you ask in general whether any personal documents were held by SUP Prizren?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I asked the employee at the duty service of the secretariat of internal affairs in Prizren.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's not the question Mr. Stamp was asking you. He was asking you how this arose, this issue, because you weren't interested in ID cards at the border.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said in my reply that I asked them for travel documents, a valid document allowing you to cross a state border. These persons stated that they had no documents at all. To my question: Where are your documents, they said they were being held at SUP Prizren. Then I inquired whether any documents were held at the duty service of SUP Prizren, whether they were found lying around taken from anyone for any reason at all whether any documents were held at SUP Prizren. Because if they were found on their territory they would first arrive at SUP Prizren before being passed on to other services.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That answer again, I don't wish to belabour this, can you just give me one answer. You seem now to be saying while the people were there you checked SUP Prizren to see if their documents were held. I wanted to know earlier and I asked you when did you check and you said after they had left. So I will ask you again. When did you check to see if SUP Prizren had the identifications of these -- the documents of these people?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wrote an official note about that incident. Those persons came to the border crossing at 12.30 and they left the territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia at 1430. So for two or two and a half hours we were in contact with Albanian state authorities because of their attempt --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... SUP Prizren?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Let him answer the question, Your Honour. He's answering the question that counsel asked him specifically. I think that counsel is starting really to step the line as to what is proper cross and what is just interrupting the witness and trying to disrupt the record of these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I asked the witness a simple question, when did he check with SUP Prizren.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And that's what he's answering. If you listen, that's what he's starting to answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Witness, I want to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a moment, Mr. Stamp, until we allow Mr. Ivetic a moment to calm down. The witness does appear to be getting to the answer at the stage where you interrupted. So can you deal with that question again, please, Mr. Ognjenovic. When did you check to see if SUP Prizren had the identification documents of these people? You should be able to tell us that in a fairly short answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] An hour after they left the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I take it you are aware that these people -- well, withdrawn, question withdrawn. Let's have a look at P3086. Is it up -- yes. Is this an official note that you compiled on the 27th of March, 1999?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And were you shown this document or told about this document since you came here?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's my document, I wrote it, and I have it with me. I know it. It's my document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you just read the second paragraph there where it speaks about 1230 hours on the 27th of March, 1999.

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "At 1230 hours on 27 March 1999, at the border crossing of Vrbnica, a group of Albanians turned up wanting to cross the Yugoslav-Albanian border without travel documents, ID cards, or any other documents. They stated that their ID cards have been taken from them and kept at the Prizren SUP."

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, firstly, you will note, sir, that you do not record in this document that four men said their ID cards were taken; the document seems to indicate that you are saying that all of them told you that their documents had been taken. Isn't that a fair assessment of what is written here, that they told you, that is, the Albanians who turned up, that their documents had been seized?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. An official note is normally made after the fact, after an event. It is a record that gives a general account of what happened. By telephone I informed the concerned people of what was going on in the meantime. Most of those people I knew because those were mainly people I knew personally and played sports with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes --

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were very few men who were driving tractors, et cetera. The rest were all women and children.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What I want to ask you and what I ask you firstly about this document is that from this record that you made, is it still your testimony that four men said that they did not have travel documents -- or four men say that their travel documents had been seized or that all of them said that their documents had been seized? Looking at the record that you made.

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't talk with all the hundred people. Those who knew me came to see me personally. I talked to them, interviewed them, asked for their travel documents. I wasn't able to talk to every woman and child there. Later on when I wrote that official note, I wrote that they had no documents at all. When talking to them, I asked them only about travel documents; but later, when I wrote the official note, I formulated it as no documents at all because most of them --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Now, those that you spoke to told you that their travel documents had been seized by the Prizren SUP?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't say they were taken away from them. He said they were kept there -- maybe they were lying to me, maybe nobody stopped them on the road at all, maybe they just wanted to get out as soon as possible. I didn't search any of them, anyone, not women and not children, and the children were small, 3 or 5 years old. You don't expect me to ask them for ID, do you?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: How many of them told you that the Prizren SUP had seized their documents? How many told you that?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those who talked to me. I'll give you a number. The two who played football with me, who came to see me in my office. I sat with them for an hour talking. They told me on behalf of everyone else. I didn't talk to everyone. I couldn't talk to everyone and I wasn't interested in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, ten minutes after they arrived there, that's at 1240 -- or perhaps I could ask you, please read the second or the third paragraph of this note that you made: "At 1240 hours ..."

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "At 1240, SUP Prizren and the MUP of the Republic of Serbia - the administration of border police - were informed by telephone. Approval was received to allow the aforesaid persons to leave for Albania."

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, when you spoke to the SUP, the Prizren SUP at 1240, did you inform them or inquire about these identification or these documents which these persons that you played football with were sitting in your office for over an hour told you had been seized by the police?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the secretariat of internal affairs in Prizren, there is a department of border police. They have a direct line to the border. I informed them, because they are the competent secretariat on that territory, and this matter concerned citizens of Prizren, I informed them that I have in my office persons who want to cross the border without any travel documents. I wasn't interested in IDs or anything else. They had no travel documents. Later on in that official note I covered all sorts of documents, all types; but at that moment when I was talking to them I was only interested in travel documents, because travel documents such as passport are the only legal type of document allowing you to cross the state border.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Sir, the question is: While these people were in your office for over an hour, according to you, these people --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- just give us a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Stamp, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Just to get back to the context. These persons were in breach of the law on identifications. These persons were people that you knew well, they were sitting in your office for over an hour. Many of them, you said, were women and children in a distressed condition. You had to spend hours. You said it took you three visits or three contacts with the general on the Albanian side while they waited at the border post to get them to cross. Why is it when these people were sitting in your office did you not inquire of the Prizren SUP about the travel documents?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, the way the question is phrased, just to get back into context, if counsel wants to have the full context, he must state the full context. He must take into account also the testimony yesterday that a majority of the Kosovo Albanians, especially women and children, did not possess passports and only males did that. That's the testimony that was on the record yesterday, and if counsel's question is going to say let's get into the context, we need the full context instead of having counsel take things out of context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Look, though, Mr. Ivetic, at the question. The question is at the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I agree, but it comes with that caveat, let's get things into context. If we're going to use caveats like that, they must mean something, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Indeed, but the question doesn't require the proposition that you've just suggested has to be added into this narrative. Indeed, one has to ask the question from here why this particular question doesn't just consist of the last two lines. But, Mr. Stamp, please -- you may continue with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Why is it you did not while these people were at the border post inquire of your colleagues at the SUP Prizren about the documents which these people told you were seized by SUP Prizren?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As they arrived at the border crossing, they came to my office and said that they had no documents; then I dialled the number. I cannot cover all that in the official note. It's -- the official note is just a general outline. I had to call on the phone and find out what exactly is the procedure because it was the first time that people wanted to go to Albania. So I asked in Belgrade what to do about these Siptars who wanted to go to Albania. They told me, You have your own administration, see what to do with them. So I was told to concentrate on my administration, the only one that's competent for border affairs. That's when I told them they had no documents. That's the administration of border affairs at the SUP Prizren. I didn't ask the duty service immediately. I contacted the duty service only after they had left. Those are two different services in the SUP, the one I called, the border police department and the duty service. Those are not the same crews.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, I understand that, but -- and the question really is: Why is it you didn't inquire of the duty service or the relevant people in SUP Prizren about the documents which these people claimed had been seized by SUP Prizren?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, perhaps it was my omission, that I didn't do it right away. I asked later. It was a surprise for all of us for these people to appear there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know of any valid reason that the police in Prizren could have had to seize these people's travel documents or these people's personal documentation?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no reason, and I don't believe that anyone seized the documents. They just told me that in order to leave our territory as soon as possible. Probably no one stopped them or checked them on the road, I am sure of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we look at the fourth paragraph of your record you say that: "A total of 94 people, women and elderly, crossed over. We took their personal details as they stated them and finger-printed them all." Is that a correct record of what you did?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's how it was. I took it for me, it was not an official action, just so that I could later have a list of who left the country. I took their finger-print and their names so that I knew who were the people who left, so that I had a document for myself of the persons who left the territory. It was the first case of people leaving our territory. It means that it was not an official action. I did that just for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Stamp. Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, a part of the answer that the witness gave was not entered into the transcript. He said he took the finger-prints of the people who were of age, that he assumed should have had the travel documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ognjenovic, where is the list of the names of these people and where are their finger-print records?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The documents were in my office, with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Where are they now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I assume you would send a copy of this to your administration in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I didn't send it because it was not an official action. I did that for my own security. It was not my duty to do that. I only did that for me and it was left in my office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm not following you, I'm sorry. What's it got to do with your security?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not security, it has nothing to do with security, but to provide a justification for my actions, to have a record of people who had left the territory of the FRY, and this is why I took the finger-print. This is why I did that, for my own reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, you have me completely lost. I would be grateful if you could assist me. Why would you keep a personal copy of people's finger-prints? Sorry, Mr. Zecevic has an intervention.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, a part of his answer was not entered into transcript again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And you say it was?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It was that he says: I needed a justification for letting these -- this group of people without travelling documents passing the border. That is why I did it. That is what he says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. It doesn't help me, I'm afraid. I still have no idea why you would want to keep a personal record of finger-prints of people crossing the border.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I took it because if after a certain amount of time these ID cards were found, then using those finger-prints we could establish that these were those people. This is the reason why I took the finger-print because when personal ID cards are issued finger-prints are taken. So if this was found then we would know who left the territory. We didn't know that columns would start arriving later. So then people started leaving en masse, so we didn't do this anymore, only the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll have a read at this again later, but it was your reference to you did it for yourself, whether you used the word security or not, and it's that I'm trying to understand. I can understand you doing it officially as you've described, but why did you say you had done it for yourself personally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did it because the action that I did, I permitted people who do not possess documents, valid documents to leave the country to leave the country; that is why I did it. They did not meet the conditions to be able to leave the country. This is why I did that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, I think this is a suitable opportunity to deal with an issue that is concerning the Bench, and that is that statements are constantly being made from the Defence side of this case that can be -- that are audible and they are made not only in English but they are made in what is described in this institution as B/C/S, or here Serbian. The Bench wish to ensure that witnesses are not being prompted by comments made from the Defence, whether in the heat of the moment or deliberately doesn't matter for this purpose at the present moment. So I ask all involved to restrain themselves from making audible comments of any kind during the course of the evidence of any witness, and this direction applies to counsel, all lawyers, and other legal staff in court, and to the accused themselves, because there are examples of all being involved in this. Now, please continue, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Let's move on, but before we leave this document, if you look at the bottom of the document you will see handwritten, and it is on page 2 of the English, handwritten, if we could move to page 2, sent to MUP of the Republic of Serbia, UPP, that's -- I think you said that's your department; the Pristina MUP staff. Why was this sent to the Pristina MUP staff?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wrote this by hand at the bottom so that I know to whom I sent this official note. I sent it to the MUP of the Republic of Serbia, the border crossing administration, as those authorised; and to the rest I sent for their information, to the staff, to the state security centre, in order for them to inform themselves about it. And one copy was left for the station. So the MUP, as the authorised party, and the rest of the parties for their information only. Each action that is done at the border crossing must be recorded and certain services need to be informed about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Was it a requirement that you should inform the MUP staff of actions like the one you had taken?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter would like the witness to repeat his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could you repeat that answer, please. The interpreter did not catch it. I think I caught it but the interpreter didn't.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We informed the staff only for their information. We didn't have any obligation to, just for their information. It was not something that derived from an order. That's why I said that official notes were written in four or five copies so that we would inform the others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I thought your answer was "ne," but it was obviously a bit more complicated. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can we look quickly at 6D666.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This is a document that was on the list of documents to be used by the Defence but has not been used. I just want to ask one question about it before I move on. Now, there is translation for this. Can I just ask you -- or I could just indicate, this is a document of the 3rd of April, 1999, and you see where it says "official note," can you read that and the succeeding sentence for me aloud, please.

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Drafted by the head of the staff of General -- of Major-General Sreten Lukic on the order conveyed to the SUP chiefs in the autonomous province of Kosovo and Metohija in relation to the manner of behaviour of members of the police." Should I read on?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, I just wanted -- is this -- have you seen documents like this before referring to orders that were issued by the MUP staff or by General Lukic to SUP chiefs?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could have seen this only if I were at the chief of the SUP Prizren secretariat Milos Vojinovic that would be the only time I would be aware of this. As for orders of how we should act at the border crossing was something that we could only be ordered by our SUP in Belgrade. So this didn't really refer to us. I could only have been informed about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. During -- and I'm moving on --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: One correction for the transcript, Your Honours, line 20 of this page he informed the -- I think the word he used was "uprava," which would be the administration in Belgrade, not the SUP in Belgrade -- or it might have been the MUP. I apologise but maybe we can clarify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think you must be right, Mr. Ivetic, and we note what you say. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you recall in the course of the -- of 1999, as a matter of fact, on the 9th of May, 1999, your border post being visited by members of the press?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, this was on the 7th of May, not on the 9th of May. A group of journalists came numbering eight persons. Among them was David Davi, who introduced himself as an advisor of Jacques Chirac. Together with them there were also two members of the SUP, members of the Prizren secretariat for internal affairs. They came to me, they entered my office, and we had some talks for some 15 minutes or so. Then we actually came to the border, we returned, and then they went in the direction of Prizren. David Bowie, I think that's what his name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: He's a popular singer. Are you suggesting that he was a journalist and also a --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I'm sorry, I made a mistake about the name. It's Resid Davi, that was his name, Resid Davi, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: How's his singing? Are you suggesting that this person was both a journalist and a government advisor to the French government or was he different from the others?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The name Resid Davi, that's how he introduced himself. I didn't know who he was. He just introduced himself as an advisor of President Jacques Chirac. I didn't ask him anything more. Again, I'm not sure about the name, but I think that was it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Could we have a look at P3091.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could be heard on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: This document was only intimated to us a few days ago, but we have several concerns with it. First of all, this does not appear to be --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can this be dealt without -- or should it be dealt with with the witness out of court?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: For the sake of things, we probably should. I would rather err on the side of caution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We have a matter of law to deal with, Mr. Ognjenovic. Could you please leave the court while we deal with this

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: First of all, we don't know the providence of this document. It appears to be someone's recitation or recollection of an AFP service that, according to this information, appears to have been broadcast rather than a printed report, so we don't know whether this is actually a news report or not. We've had problems with news reports and recollections by journalists in this case already and documents have been questioned or some have even been denied admission based upon that ground. But in this case, this is not even an official publication. This is, I suspect, what the Prosecution has in the past done, is give us documents from a certain government agency in the United States that is closely linked with the intelligence sector, which identifies documents for -- which spreads documents for what would be called propaganda circumstances here. This particular document also for me is somewhat troubling in that there appears to be some sort of redaction in the upper left-hand corner of the same that is not explained and makes it impossible to undertake any steps to completely verify this document, if indeed it can be verified, so the number -- the time has passed and the inability to know the exact source of the said document. And there are comments at the bottom of the document indicating that this is not an original-source document because it describes that this is a -- a -- someone's recollection or transcript of the independent French press agency, Agence France-Presse. I submit that without bringing the person -- so we don't know whether this is transcribed properly from transmission of Agence France-Presse or not and it causes great issue as to whether what is represented in here is authentically represented or not, but even apart from the usual concerns relating to newspaper articles and news coverage of events in general.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can we have it on the screen, please. Magnify it, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And it goes without saying that the text of the article does not support the title or the by-line, as it would be called if there were a written publication, which it's not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What's the question or the line of questioning that you wish to pursue, Mr. Stamp?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This is a news report of the interview which the witness just spoke of, and it quotes him as saying certain things. And it refers to certain things that the news reporter observed. The line of questioning is whether or not this is an accurate news report, if he remembers saying these things and if the circumstances that the reporter observed are correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I can make just one more submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry. I thought you were finished.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The testimony of the witness thus far has not identified any such interview. He said that he talked with this Resid Davi or whatever -- the person who has a similar name to a singer, let's leave it at that for purposes of clarity. But I don't believe that there's been any evidence that an actual interview took place or, for the matter, that there's been any contact with news journalists that has been elicited from this witness. And there's also an issue where there are two dates mentioned in this document and it's unclear, at least to me, whether we're talking about an incident on the 9th of May or the 7th of May, since both dates are identified in this report and thus far this Aleksandar Mitic who's referenced here has not been identified as having been present at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The witness has already said it was the 7th of May

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, we think your objection is misplaced. All the points you've made are good arguments, let me put it that way, if you were resisting the presentation of this as a free-standing document. But what it's being used for is to refresh the memory of the witness with a view to seeing how much of this he agrees with or disagrees with. And only to the extent that he accepts it will it become evidence in the case. We are not going to treat this at this stage as free-standing material that contradicts him. So on that basis we reject the objection and we'll allow the line to be pursued. We can have the witness back, please. Could we have the witness back, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you for your patience. Thank you for your patience. The matter's now been dealt with and we can proceed. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This visit you had from the journalist on the 7th of May, do you recall if one of them or a member of the party was Aleksandar Mitic?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you recall that some of the journalists were from the Agence France-Presse?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The journalists who went there, did they interview you in your office? You said you met with some of them in your office.

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't an interview. It was a conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, in front of you is a document. Do you read English at all?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The document purports to be a report of what you said to journalists, and the report is that on the left side of the border -- sorry. Can you hear now?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The report is that there was a pile of licence plates scattered on the ground at the left side of the border check-point. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And the report quotes you as saying: "'We are taking the licence plates away because we do not want the Kosovo Liberation Army to come back in these cars pretending to be refugees.'" Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly didn't state it in those terms. It depends on how he took my words, but I never stated anything of the sort. I don't know anything about the reason for licence plates or the return.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, did you tell them anything in relation to the taking of licence plates?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In an informal conversation, when we talked in the office, I never mentioned nor would I mention, nor did we confiscate any document whatsoever or any licence plates. People discarded them on their own. I would have never stated anything of the sort nor did we ever do this. We just found these things in the area of the border crossing. We did not confiscate them. There was a pile of licence plates on the left side. I immediately wrote an official note about this, not only about this but about whatever happened at the border crossing and then I forwarded this to competent authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you also speak to them about identification cards?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I spoke about ID cards as well, about all events and all observations that were of interest to them. It was an informal conversation, it was no interview, nothing was written down. We just sat down and talked informally, exchanged opinion, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You're recorded here as saying: "'Most Albanians threw their identity cards in our faces saying: 'We don't want this trash.''" ? Did you tell them that?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were such cases, perhaps, I'm not sure, but there were such cases. Not just IDs, any documents that they had issued by the Republic of Serbia was thrown away by them, especially after crossing the borderline. It did happen, they threw everything away. They cursed, they made provocations, and they did all that after crossing the border.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So you might have told them -- told them that?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The report goes on to say: "But he added," that is you, that is you said, "that identity papers were sometimes taken away from those crossing into Albania." Didn't you tell them that identification cards were sometimes taken away?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That you also said -- or did you also say: "'They say they do not respect this country. If you don't respect your country and you spit on it, you do not need the papers.'" ? Do you recall telling them that?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. I don't know how they translated that. I speak only Serbian. Perhaps we didn't understand each other linguistically.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm just asking if you remember saying that. When -- did you tell --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- one moment. Did you not tell us that you spoke fluent Albanian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Albanian, yes, but they didn't speak Albanian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Perhaps we should have a translation of page 25, lines 12 to 14 from CLSS. Please continue, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Hysni Kryeziu, your neighbour, came here and testified to the same thing, that -- or similar things. Do you recall seeing him when he crossed the border into Albania?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember, I do. Every resident of my village who left the country asked for me and said good-bye to me personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And so you remember asking him what happened to his car?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, you noticed that he and those members of his family that accompanied him were on foot, were trekking on foot out of their country into Albania?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were such cases. There also were cases where people had deserted their cars on the road and continued on foot. They didn't want to wait in the column any longer. They just abandoned their vehicle and continued on foot. There were such cases, and I can't remember because there were so many people and I can't remember to who I spoke about what. But I remember seeing him and talking to him. I know him very well. He's a neighbour of mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: He said that while he was there he saw policemen taking money from people, taking away people's cars and documents, and taking off the licence plates of cars. Wasn't that, in fact, occurring at that post or in the vicinity of that post while you were there?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see that. Had there been such cases I would have taken action against those who did that. I'm 100 per cent sure that had this been done to any of the people, they would have come to see me to complain to me, the people leaving the country, because they trusted me enough to come to me to complain; however, nobody came to complain about the conduct and attitude of policemen at the border crossing. I'm 100 per cent of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Hysni Kryeziu left Albania on the 27th of April. Another witness, Lizane Malaj, was expelled, according to her testimony, on the 27th of April and may I correct myself, Kryeziu was expelled on the 27th of March. Another witness, Lizane Malaj, passed through your border post on the 27th of April and she said that that conduct by the police there of seizing people's identification documents and licence plates was continuing up till that time. Isn't that true, sir?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't have such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: After you were visited by these journalists on the 7th of May, did you ever see a news report or hear of a news report that they published in respect to their visit to the border post?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In your discussion with journalists, was there any mention made of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What was said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They asked, Why aren't there any young men? And I told them, Most likely they are in the KLA and they do not leave the territory of Kosovo. They remain while they sent their families out of the country. They inquired about all of the events there, and then we went out together to the borderline and they found their journalists on the Albanian side. Our journalists talked to them who were on the Albanian side, they talked, and then we took them to the borderline to see the barricades, to see the people crossing. They wanted to see why -- why was there a bottleneck, why was there a delay; and the Albanian side started recording all the people crossing the border. This is why there was a huge backup on our side of the border.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And is that all that was said about the KLA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember. Perhaps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I ask because it might seem to some people a very good reason for taking the registration plates to avoid the vehicles being used to bring KLA fighters back into the country, but you didn't say that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could Albanians or any other person for that matter return to the country without identification papers or travel documents?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already said that that wasn't a regular procedure. We didn't control or check on any passengers. There were cases where people came back and went back to their homes. There were such cases. I think that I even quoted an example to them where a group of our citizens had returned on that day or on a previous day. I don't remember because it wasn't so busy. But I think that there was an example where a smaller group had come back and gone home. There were such cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. Could Albanians enter the country without identification or travel documents at your border post?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already said that under regular circumstances, no, it would have been impossible; but the situation wasn't regular. The documents were not checked when people were crossing the border, going in and going out, because it was so busy. We didn't have enough personnel, nor was it possible to have regular checks. But naturally they came and they said that they wanted to go back to their homes and we allowed them but without any control whatsoever. We let them in but we didn't check on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I have nothing further from this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stamp. Mr. Stamp, the document that you referred to P3086, what's the date of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That's the 27th of March, if I could just confirm. 3086 is dated the 27th of March.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And what about 6D1497, that's also the 27th of March. Are these two documents identical?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. If you -- if I could be of assistance. The P3086 is number 71 and the other one is number 72. Yesterday he testified that there -- relating to this 71 and 72 with respect to this incident. They're talking about the same incident; they're not identical documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I was actually looking for a note from yesterday which must be inconsistent with -- or at least about which my recollection must be wrong. I thought something was said yesterday about it being possible to return to the country without a passport. Is that an inaccurate recollection of what was said yesterday, Mr. Ivetic? Can you help me?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd obviously -- I'd obviously defer to the transcript. I don't have a chance to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's all right. I for some reason can't find the note, so my recollection must be wrong. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ognjenovic, the first group of people trying to leave the country arrived on the 27th of March at your border post and then there were a series of people leaving, and you told us of efforts you made to persuade these ones to return. Did you try to persuade other groups to return?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did try. In the first group I knew a lot of people and I asked them three or four times to go back. And then in other columns that arrived, whenever I knew people, I asked them to go back, also my neighbours, I asked them not to go, telling them there was no need to leave the territory; however, they were persistent and they left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Had you been given orders to tell them to turn back?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Bearing in mind the explanation you've given, that they were in danger from NATO bombs, why did you want them to go back?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How should I say it? NATO didn't bomb houses. They bombed military facilities, but out of fear, out of there being a possibility for them to be attacked, they believed they were safer if they went to Albania, that was their opinion. I asked them to stay, telling them that it wasn't so, but they probably had some sort of an order telling them all to leave in order to cause a humanitarian catastrophe so that they would all be in one place. And as we can see, they have succeeded in that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So are you saying the official position, government position was that NATO bombs will hit only military targets so you'll be safe in your houses?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, that was just my opinion because I have experienced all of this myself and that's why I'm saying so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you clarify as best you can the time at which the road immediately before the border crossing was mined?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the exact date, but I think it was towards the end of our withdrawal. Anti-tank barricades had been set up earlier, and as for mining, that was done towards the end of our pull-out, perhaps late May. I'm not sure of the exact date, perhaps even a bit earlier. I'm not sure. I don't remember the date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So the family that was killed from Pristina, was that in late May?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date. I don't remember, but that was just a little bit before then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You've given us a lot of detail about events at the border, and laying mines along the side of the road must have been one of the most significant things that happened there about which you would have to take protective measures. Have you no recollection of when that was?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember the date. It was only the tip of the border crossing area that was mined, at the very edge of the border, because if you look at the terrain, on one side we have Pastrik mount, on the other side we have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just answer my question, please. Whether it was one mine or 101 mines, it was obviously an important danger to be avoided by any police officers on duty. You said that once that happened, there was a VJ presence?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Army of Yugoslavia came after the on-site investigation was done in order to de-mine the remaining area, after the investigation was conducted by the Prizren SUP personnel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, I got the impression that there was a presence of the VJ to guide people away from the mines at the side of the road.

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to my information, the army was alongside the road from the village of Zub [as interpreted] to Vrbnica, and in the area of the border crossing there wasn't a single member of the Army of Yugoslavia except for those people employed at my station.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So why were they lined along the road from Zub to Vrbnica?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I think it was in order to ensure that people wouldn't turn off the road, so that they wouldn't hit a mine. We had a police patrol where people were injured when they took a turn off the road. It was a police patrol of the Zur police department and two policemen were injured or killed on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now we have two references there. Zub and Zur are two separate places, are they?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zub is near Djakovica and Zur is in Prizren municipality, 6 kilometres from the border crossing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, so what we've been discussing so far is the road from Zur to Vrbnica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, are you saying there were mines along the side of that road for a distance of 6 kilometres?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm not aware of that. I know that there were, but I wasn't present in order to know this myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, you've just told me that the VJ were there to keep people away from mines.

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about the Zur-Vrbnica road. There were patrols, a patrol, perhaps a patrol passed, warned people when there -- whenever we had traffic congestions there would be a patrol coming to regulate traffic. So it would be congested. So we tried to avoid catastrophe at any cost --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ognjenovic, I am talking about VJ. Now, you're not telling me, are you, that the VJ were directing the traffic? So let's stick to the point, please. What I want to know is whether there were mines along the road from Zur to the border crossing at Vrbnica.

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And I thought that's what you told us yesterday, and what I was trying to establish is when these mines were laid.

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, at one point you were going to tell me that mines were laid for only a very short distance before the border. Is that a separate mine-laying arrangement or exercise?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was in the area of the border crossing, not along the road, but in the border crossing area. I told you that four mines, or I don't know how many were laid, only in a very limited area where there was a possibility to cross in from the territory of Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, intervening for the transcript, he used the term -- I don't know if it would be in line 13 or 14, but "kopnene," which we've had before which is for infantry to cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, yesterday's note I have is that there were two exit lanes to the bridge at the border. The left lane was mined and there were anti-tank barricades. And then you said that there was for a distance of 6 kilometres on both sides of the road from the Zur intersection to the border, there were also mines. That's correct, is it?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were mines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And these mines were laid by the VJ?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, what I'd like to know is what was the extent of the presence of the VJ along the road between the Zur intersection and the border.

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of how many of them there were, but I did see them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, were they along -- were they in a visible line along both sides of the road all the way? Were they at a check-point? What was the distribution of the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there was no check-point. When I was passing by in my car, I saw them going, walking, on the road. I don't know what they were saying to the passengers. I just saw them in that section. I don't even know whether they were soldiers from the border post or from some other unit. I just saw them as I passed by.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And they were there every day?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember about every day, but I did used to see them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, were they there to prevent people straying into the areas mined?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said I didn't know why they were there. I didn't ask them. They didn't report to me. They didn't stop me. We had no contact. I just saw them. I don't know what their assignment was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And when did this -- these VJ soldiers first appear on that road on a regular basis?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know which day it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you not tell me roughly when it was, try to help us get to the truth of all this?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know. Most probably as soon as the column of refugees started to form, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now can you help me with the working arrangements in the Prizren SUP. What were the normal office hours of the Prizren SUP?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what the office hours were, the office hours were 24 hours/7, the SUP is always open, but I can only speak about my own station, Prizren, I don't know about the other SUPs. I was only talking about my own post.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And that's all I've asked you about.

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my station it was organized 24/7 --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: There might be an error in the translation. The B/C/S wasn't exactly what Your Honour said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'll ask the question again. What were the normal office hours of the SUP Prizren?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know about SUP Prizren.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You've indicated that there would be occasions when you had to contact that office. You as a serving police officer, albeit in a different department, did not know anything about the opening hours of the SUP Prizren; is that your position?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I know about the office hours of SUP Prizren. I don't know what you're interested in because the border police administration worked from 7.00 to 1500 hours, that's the department that I was working for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There must be a translation problem. It sounds so simple in English, though, and I'll ask the question for the third time. What were the normal office hours of the SUP Prizren?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: SUP Prizren is a broad concept. There are uniformed police who worked 24 hours a day, the duty service works 24 hours a day, the department to which I reported worked normal hours, from 7.00 to 3.00 p.m. It was directly connected with my post, that is the department of border police within the secretariat of internal affairs in Prizren.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, 7.00 to 3.00 p.m. how many days a week?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Monday to Friday, Monday through Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The 27th of March was a Saturday. Can you tell me how you managed to make contact with someone in SUP Prizren in your -- in the building in your border post section there?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The department of border affairs is directly linked to us, that means that anything that happens within a period of 24 hours from Sunday to Sunday, we were able to contact them. We had a contact telephone number and a contact person. If they were not in their -- at their desk, we had a telephone number to find them wherever they were. We were able to contact them at any time, including Saturday or Sunday, but their regular hours were Monday through Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you now tell me then what happened on the 27th of March again so that we can be clear about it.

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the whole incident?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, about the contacts you made and who you spoke to. We know the events as you've described them, but we'd like to be clear about who you contacted and how you made these contacts.

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the passengers arrived to the border crossing, I informed the administration of border police in Belgrade immediately. I explained to them why I was calling and asked what to do next with them, what to do with the persons who were at that time standing at the border crossing. The answer I got was that if Albanian border authorities allow those persons to cross the border, I should let them go. I had three contacts with Albanian border authorities, and when they said that these persons could come over I allowed them to cross the border. And then I informed SUP Prizren about the event. I informed personally the section chief Ljubomir [as interpreted] Zdravkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The name, I think the witness said Miomir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you repeat the name of the person who was the chief, section chief.

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Miomir Zdravkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, at one stage earlier today you told Mr. Stamp that you spoke to the border police office in the SUP building. That's missing from the account you've just given us. Can you clarify for us, please, what contact you had on Saturday, the 27th of March, 1999, with the border police office within the SUP building.

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The workers of the border police office work in mufti, they are operative offices, but the duty service in Prizren is manned by uniformed police. I informed them just to inform them that there was an incident at the border crossing that such and such things happened. That's the reason why I called them, to inform them all. It was just for their information that I contacted the border police office and all the other services, but I asked for instructions from my administration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic may wish to re-examine you on this to -- if he can help us further from his own more extensive knowledge of the circumstances. I have just one final question at this stage. You have regularly used the expression "travel documents" in answers you've given rather than the word "passport." Can you explain to me why you use the expression "travel documents" and indeed what you mean by "travel documents"?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Travel document and a passport, those are the same things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Was it possible in any circumstances to travel across the border from Serbia to either Albania or Macedonia with a document other than a passport or a combination of documents other than a passport?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What -- with what combination of documents?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One can cross the border also carrying a lesse passe. A lesse passe is normally issued to a person who is stranded abroad without a passport. They are issued with a lesse passe to enable them to come back to their home country. Also, a tourist card can be issued to a person on the border if they produce a valid ID, that tourist card is valid for 30 days. There are also minor border passes, people who live in the border area can move from one state to another, cross the border frequently with a border pass unless otherwise stipulated by an international agreement. Yugoslavia and Bulgaria had a border that local residents in the border belt were able to cross on national holidays to visit family, et cetera, without any documents in certain sections. One can cross the border without any documents in case of a natural disaster such as a war, a flood, an earthquake, things like that, without that being considered as an illegal crossing of the border. Those are exceptional cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could a Kosovar Albanian with a valid identity card obtain a tourist card to cross into Albania for a limited period of time, and thus cross without a passport?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tourist cards were something we issued to enable people to get into our country, not out of our country. We issued tourist cards only for incoming passengers who wanted to come for tourist purposes. They had to produce tourist vouchers from tour operators, and then on the basis of that we could decide whether to issue them the tourist card or not. But first we had to contact our administration in Belgrade to get approval and we have a record kept about the tourist cards issued.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does that mean that you're saying that the only way in which a Kosovar Albanian can visit Albania in normal circumstances is with a passport?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. We need to have a break now, Mr. Ognjenovic, so could you please leave the courtroom with the usher while we have the break, and we will resume at 20 minutes past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, does anything arise for you from these questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Re-examination, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if you allow me, perhaps one question follows from the cross-examination that is relevant, and you asked several questions along that line. So I would like to show this witness one document that could clarify this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is it a document that he will know anything about?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a military document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, but can you answer my question --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- is it a document he will know anything about? You say he will?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document describes an event in which members of the MUP were killed on that route, and he testified precisely about this. The incident in which members of the police were killed on that route that we were discussing, Prizren-Vrbnica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is Vrbnica-Zur.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What then is to be your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Whether regarding the movement of refugees and other persons along that route he received perhaps some information from members of the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. We shall allow you to proceed that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 5D891, please, could we call that up in e-court. Further cross-examination by Mr. Cepic:

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While we are waiting, Mr. Ognjenovic, just one question. You testified that members of the MUP were killed on Vrbnica-Prizren road, they ran on a mine, a land-mine, along that road. Would you look at the first paragraph here. It was recorded that on the 17th of April, 1999, some MUP members were killed. Is that the incident you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ognjenovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ognjenovic, hello again. When talking about the incident on the 27th of March where the group of persons came without the necessary -- without travel documents or passports, you indicated at transcript page 38, line 10 through 11, to Judge Bonomy that you informed personally the section chief Miomir Zdravkovic. Where was he the section chief of the -- where was he the section chief?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was not the chief of that branch. He was chief of the section.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And where was that, was that in Belgrade or at the level ...

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was chief of sector of the department of border police in SUP Prizren, so it's a department within the secretariat of internal affairs in Prizren.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, focusing for a moment on the Vrbnica border crossing. Could you tell us how much distance was there between the Yugoslav exit ramp and the Albanian entry ramp at the Vrbnica border crossing area?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The distance was approximately 250 up to 300 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And do I understand correctly that the actual physical border, the so-called red line, is within and somewhere in the middle of this inter-area between the two ramps?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The red line is on the bridge roughly between these two roadblocks.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in this inter-area between the two ramps, are your police officers or the Albanian authorities on that side of the border, are they -- are they in this area when civilian traffic is crossing the actual red line?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were policemen there, both ours and theirs, as required, to warn people or children if they were running in that area not to veer off the road. Our policemen and Albanians did the same thing. It was not the primary reason why the policemen were there. We had to do it because of the anti-tank mines and the barricades.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, the question I have for you is that at page 24 of the transcript, first at lines 7 through 8 and then lines 20 through 24, when talking about the documentation and the plates that the persons leaving or crossing the border would discard, am I correct that the discarding of these items occurred after they had passed the Yugoslav exit ramp, and in fact after they crossed the red line and entered into Albanian territory?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Ivetic, we would very much like it if you would refrain from asking leading questions on significant matters in re-examination. It is not a helpful way to deal with the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm trying to -- I believe I'm reading back the testimony that he's already given on cross-examination. I don't recall from -- whether this was from Mr. Stamp or the Chamber, but if you look at the lines that I've referenced --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, if that's what he says, you don't need to ask him again. If you want it verified, then you must ask the question: Where was it that they deposited the material? It's a very simple exercise, not rocket science.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Where were the personal documentation and the licence plates found that you testified that you collected and took the other steps that you testified to?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These discarded objects could be found in the entire area of the border crossing. There were even cases when people took off their licence plates, put them in the boot of their car. Such things happened too.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: While Mr. Ivetic is preparing his next question, can I go back to the first matter he had asked you about, where I had clearly misunderstood part of the earlier answer. Where was it you were able to contact Miomir Zdravkovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that very moment I contacted the duty service, and they gave me Zdravkovic's telephone number so that I can inform him; and I immediately informed him by telephone. The duty service has a list of numbers for duty officers at the secretariat. I got his contact number and immediately informed Miomir Zdravkovic about the situation that has occurred at the border crossing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I have no further questions for this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just on the same subject, Mr. Ognjenovic, who was it that you spoke to in the SUP Prizren office about the identity cards and whether they had them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I asked the employee at the duty service of SUP Prizren.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Ognjenovic, that completes your evidence. Thank you for coming here to give evidence. You may now leave the courtroom with the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Our next witness is Dragan Milenkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting for the witness I could raise a preliminary matter, Your Honour, so that we don't waste time later. I don't know whether the Prosecution intends to utilise this document in cross-examination, but they did send a copy of the document to us saying that it was going to be with respect to this particular witness. It's a document that came into this case approximately one year ago, at which time another witness was testifying and at which time there had been an issue of Ms. Kandic, Natasa Kandic, in Belgrade making public certain information that had been subject to non-disclosures, and at that point in time I believe it was Mr. Marcussen had indicated that his office was very interested and concerned with finding out where their leak was for this. And I to date have not heard any of the results of their inquiries or investigations, except for the fact that the same document is now being given to me for use with this witness. So I would inquire what the results of the investigation were to discover who at the OTP side, whether it was the OTP or the witness that came here to testify, leaked information to Natasa Kandic that was subject to a non-disclosure order of this Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There are two perhaps separate issues here, Mr. Ivetic. First of all, what's the number of the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
