utterances.text: The one that was disclosed to me does not have a number. I believe in -- I believe a year ago we did give it a 6D number. One moment, sir. Now we're getting the information that it's P03092.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What's your objection to the use of the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, apart from it being a newspaper article, I'll just say as long as it's not being submitted for the truth of the matter asserted, my inquiry is whether, in fact, there has been any follow-up on this, an issue I brought up last year, about the -- about the providence of the information that Ms. Kandic had that caused a great stir, because as I might recall indeed Ms. Kandic had more information than had been disclosed to us by the Office of the Prosecution in relation to this particular document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that may or may not be a matter for us, and therefore it's not necessary to explore the detail of this in court just now. Mr. Hannis, Mr. Ivetic is asking for the result of an investigation which he understood was to be carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, frankly, I have to confess I wasn't aware of that issue or that investigation. The purpose that I propose to use this exhibit for has to do with the photograph that's in the newspaper article, which I believe is a photograph of this witness. And it may come depending on how he answers questions, what he talks about, I may ask him if he's aware that this photograph was published in the paper in January 2007, and if so, did he take any action in response to that, et cetera, et cetera. I'm not going to ask about the contents of the article or what Natasa Kandic says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I take it that you will look into what was actually said in court before and see if there is unfinished business?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And just if so, convey the result of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. We can proceed with the witness I think, Mr. Ivetic, and if a question is asked that you deem objectionable, then no doubt you will let us know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Milenkovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading that document aloud.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You will now be examined by Mr. Ivetic on behalf of Mr. Lukic. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good day, Mr. Milenkovic. As you know, my name is Dan Ivetic, and I would ask you to briefly introduce yourself for purposes of the written record.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning. My name is Dragan Milenkovic, born 28th January 1965, in a small beautiful village called Lipovica, municipality, Serbia. Father's name Stanko, mother's name Smiljana. I finished four years of primary school in my village and graduated from the eight-year primary school in the neighbouring village, Sasala near Vlasotince. And after primary school I finished two years of secondary education in Vlasotince. I wanted to become a policeman and applied to enroll for the secondary school for internal affairs in Sremska Kamenica. After detailed vetting that applied not only to me but to my entire family, I was accepted as a cadet of that primary school in 1982. In 1984 I graduated from that school and by a decision of the then-minister of internal affairs I was assigned to become a policeman on general duties in the police station Crna Trava. I'm married to Marija and I have two sons, one of whom is a policeman employed in SUP Novi Beograd, the branch police station Bezanijska Kosa. My second son is currently in the secondary civil engineering school. He's not married. From my first son I have a grandson, two years and two months old.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, could you kindly tell us specifically about your employment within the Serbian Ministry of Interior, including the positions that you held in 1998 and 1999.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: After graduating from school, as I said before, I became a policeman on general duties at the police station of Crna Trava, where I stayed until 1997 when at my own request I was transferred to Vlasotince police station, about 40 kilometres from Crna Trava.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And did you at some point in time become a member of the PJP; and if so, when and what formation or detachment?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: I became a member of the PJP, I can't remember the exact date but it was in 1997, in the B formation, the 87 Detachment of the police as it was then.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And what about 1998 and 1999, did you remain a member of that formation or did that change?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: That changed. After a while at my own request I was transferred to A formation, 4th Company [Realtime transcript read in error "for the company"] of the 37th Detachment of the PJP.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And with respect to the 37th Detachment of the PJP, could you tell me what companies comprised that detachment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think the translation was A formation for the 4th Company of the 37th Detachment. Is that right, Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Was also -- well, let me ask him again.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Were you -- was it also -- was it the A formation or the 4th Company or both or neither? Just so that all possibilities are at play and the witness can clarify.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: It's A formation of the 37th Detachment, 4th Company of the 37 Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell me what other companies comprised the 37th PJP Detachment and where they -- where the -- where they hailed from?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: The 4th Company of the 37th Detachment consisted of six companies from Pirot, Nis, Krusevac, Prokuplje, Vranje, and Leskovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And could you tell us the manner in which the ranks of the PJP companies were filled? I apologise. There's a problem with the translation. It's back on. Let me just repeat the question for sake of clarity. How were the ranks of the PJP filled?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: The PJP company was replenished from the regular police force of the secretariat in charge.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And can you describe for us the training that you underwent as a part of the PJP of the Serbian MUP?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: Training was effected in keeping with the rules prevailing in the police force, and it consisted of theory and practical components. A company commander was in charge of carrying out the training, and he was at the same time employed by the police department in Leskovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if you could tell us what criteria were there that had to be fulfilled for one to become a member of the PJP.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: The criteria were set that each member of the PJP had to meet, these would be physical and mental fitness, conduct itself, or -- of each individual employee in the service.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And could you explain for us what would be the difference between employees of a secretariat of interior that are on the PJP list and those that are not members or not included on the PJP call-up list?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: There was no particular difference, except in terms of a small salary differential. I can give you an example. As a member of the PJP, or rather, as a member of a general duty policeman, I had hundred dinars salary. On the other hand, if I was -- were to be on the list of members of the PJP, it would be, from what I can remember, because it was a long time ago, it would be 0.45 or 42 differential, meaning that my salary would have been 110 dinars. So the difference would be these negligible 10 dinars. I'm just giving you a hypothetical example because I really don't remember specifically what the salary was.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Within the PJP company of the 37th Detachment that you were a part of, were there any volunteers, that is to say members, who had not previously been employees of the Serbian MUP?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please clarify your question. Volunteers who were not active policemen at the station where they were working.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Volunteers, that is, persons who were not employed by the police that were volunteers in your detachment or your company in 1998 or 1999 specifically?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: I state responsibly that there were no volunteers in my company.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And how about within the detachment?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: Since we -- the whole 37th Detachment in specific situations were there in its entirety, I never heard of any volunteers being members of the 37th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We have had some testimony from a Prosecution witness of some 10 or so Russian volunteers within your detachment. Based on your knowledge of the personnel that were in the detachment, do you consider that such thing to be possible in 1998 or 1999?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: This is absolutely not possible. There were no volunteers other than regular members who carried out regular duties at their home units.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, if you could just briefly describe for us what the jobs or tasks of the PJP would be when called up out of your home secretariat.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: The primary task of all members of my company when we were used outside of our home stations was to prevent violations of public law and order, major such violations, securing larger gatherings like risky football matches, capturing perpetrators of serious crimes, catching specific terrorist groups, and arresting members of such groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in 1998 or 1999 was your detachment called up for duty in the Serbian province of Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. We'll get back to that. If you could tell us now what were the specific weapons that you were trained and authorised to use as a member of the PJP when so engaged?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: As a PJP member, just like other members of my company had weapons, that was in accordance with the rules for weapons for members of the police. I had a personal side-arm, a CZ pistol and a 72-millimetre rifle. There were some others who had an M-72, 7.62-millimetre calibre machine-guns, meaning that some persons in the unit were also issued some heavier weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The transcript may or may not have caught all of that. Could you repeat what the heavier weapons were that other persons in your unit were issued.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: I already said that I was issued with a pistol, a 9-millimetre pistol, and an automatic rifle of 7.62-millimetres calibre. Some members had a M-72 machine-gun of 7.62-millimetres -- or actually, it was an M-84 of 7.62-millimetre calibre. There were also some mortars of 60-millimetre calibre and 82-millimetre calibre mortars and a special squad was trained for the use of these particular weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In the course of -- strike that. In 1998 and 1999, can you describe for us what the official uniform worn by the PJP out in the engagement and exercise of its duties was?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: Pursuant to the rules on carrying or wearing uniforms for police members, in 1998 a blue camouflage uniform was worn. I don't remember the exact date, but I think that sometime in September, I'm not sure if it was September, green camouflage uniforms were issued, which were then worn on our bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: With respect to both sets of camouflage uniforms, can you describe for us the insignia or markings on the same?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: The left shoulder was where a visible police patch was worn, then we had a blue cap or a beret with the same insignia. There was also a green combat jacket or a combat vest that had a visible sign written on the back, "policija," police. That was written in large letters that were white and it could be seen from as far as 80 to 100 metres away. As for the green camouflage uniform insignia, the sleeve was also where a PJP patch was visible, the left sleeve, and we had an emblem on our cap with two crossed swords and the emblem of Serbia and we also had a "policija" sign on the vests that was very, very easy to spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: For purposes of clarifying the transcript, at page 55, line 2, you're recorded as saying you had a blue cap or a beret. Did, in fact, you say that and did the PJP have berets?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: There were no berets. Actually, the regular-issue caps were -- that's what they were, they were caps.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think that clears up the translation issues, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, in 1998 and 1999 were there instances of non-standard uniforms or non-standard appearance by PJP members within your detachment?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: In 1998 and 1999, when I was a member of both of the formations, we had a strict order from the company commander at the time to strictly and responsibly adhere to the rules on wearing uniforms that were set down by law at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: How about personal appearance and grooming, was that also regulated strictly by the PJP company commander?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. This was strictly monitored, the manner of wearing the uniforms and personal appearance. There were only a few people, including myself, who for a while wore a beard, small beard, and this was tolerated. I wore this beard because I had serious infections on my face and I suffer the consequences from that to this very day, and all the consequences were a result of the unhygienic conditions in which we were staying.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And did that facial condition affect the ability to shave; and if so, how?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You mentioned a facial infection. Could you describe how that affected your appearance.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: It was horrible. I had some sores or scabs appear on my face and they were getting infected and there was pus which was very painful, also for the others who were close to me to look at.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And were you able to shave as a result of this infection?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: I did shave for a while, but after I would shave this would get even worse, the scabbing would get even worse. So that then I did wear a beard for as long as I could stand it, and all of this was in order to prevent the further spread of the infection that was on my face. And I am actually suffering from the effects of that infection to this very day because no beard is growing anymore on certain parts of my face.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us if at any point in time during the course of your engagement in the PJP in 1998 or 1999 whether coloured ribbons were used as part of the -- or affixed to the uniform in the course of undertaking activities?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what colour ribbons were used in 1998.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: From what I can remember, blue, yellow, and red ribbons were used.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What colour ribbons were used in 1999?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: I think that the same colours were used, blue, yellow, and red.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Were coloured ribbons used throughout 1999 or only for a certain period in 1999?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot remember precisely when the ribbons were used, but I think it was either in early or late April 1998 [as interpreted] and I believe that they were worn until the end of the war in June 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether it's a translation issue or not, but were -- when were the ribbons first utilised in the year 1999? Because the answer in the transcript talks about 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I object. The transcript says also until the end of the war in 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The question had nothing to do with 1998, and therefore the clarification's legitimate, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, when in 1999 were coloured ribbons first utilised, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: From what I know, but I'm not sure, I think they were used immediately after the war, sometime in the month of April, but again I'm repeating since this was a long time ago I don't remember everything 100 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: When you say "immediately after the war," would that be after the commencement of the war or after the conclusion of the war?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: I think that I said earlier also that this was after the start of the war, and later I can explain why these ribbons were worn.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And for the record, Your Honour, we do have Exhibit 6D761 and 6D237 which relate to the use of coloured ribbons.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us why these coloured ribbons were introduced?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can we clarify whether we're talking about 1998 or 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, unless there's a reason -- I'm --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In 1998 or 1999 why were these ribbons utilised?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: The ribbons were used for only one reason. In the field it would happen that Siptar terrorists obtained both the blue camouflage uniforms and then later the green camouflage uniforms and they would easily with those uniforms enter the facilities, houses, and the towns and the villages where members of the police were billeted or members of the army or just regular citizens, and then they would be able to commit crimes without hindrance.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Can we now focus on the time-period in 1999 when you were -- when you were sent to -- strike that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: 1998 first of all. Did you have occasion to be sent to Orahovac in Kosovo and Metohija in 1998?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us when that was?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: I really cannot say exactly what the time was, what month it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could you describe the time-period in terms of what was going on in Orahovac at the time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: When you were sent to the Orahovac area in 1998, what was the situation in Orahovac at that time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: When we as a unit were sent to carry out regular tasks and assignments in Orahovac, or rather, to help the Orahovac SUP, from what I can remember the situation was tense in the sense that people were afraid of the actions of the so-called KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Was there a period of time when the UCK activity in Orahovac increased dramatically?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In July the town of Orahovac was held by the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And did your PJP company become engaged in any activities addressed at the KLA that held the town of Orahovac in July of 1998?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us about the activities of your company relative to this time.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: In July, more specifically on the 18th of July, a part of my company was stationed on the Djakovica-Pristina section of the road near the village of Drakovina. Pursuant to orders of the company commander, a part of the unit was tasked with liberating the town of Orahovac. The company arrived on trucks to the settlement of Zrze, I believe, which is on the Prizren-Djakovica road, where we were informed by members of other units that Orahovac was under the control of the terrorists who were very well-entrenched and well-armed so that they were firing quite forcefully in the direction of our forces. For security reasons, the company commander, since he assumed that the roads were mined, my company set off towards Orahovac on foot. Naturally, by applying combat tactics, we were moving towards Orahovac. When we reached after certain time the entry point into town we heard very intense firing that was taking place in the down-town area as well as in the area that was populated exclusively by the Serbs in an area known as Vran Stena. The very entry of our people into Orahovac -- actually, I have to correct myself. At the very entry point into Orahovac I noticed several tanks of the Army of Yugoslavia which were not active at that point in time but were stationed in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Among the units taking part in this action to deblockade Orahovac, were there elements of the SAJ?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: I as a member of the reconnaissance squad was by establishment envisaged to enter first in the down-town area and in the area around it I did not register any members of the SAJ. Later on I heard that they had been there, but some 5 to 600 metres further near the settlement which was populated exclusively by Serbs, as I have told you, known as Vran Stena, which is in the direction of Malisevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you happen to see any dead civilians near any fuel stations or gas stations in Orahovac?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object. That's leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Undoubtedly leading, Mr. Ivetic. Please try to ask open questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Were there any fuel stations in Orahovac --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You know that that's not the way to ask that question. You know you've picked up the wrong part of it to ask an open question. Move to something else. It's now valueless.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I apologise but under the conditions we've been working under, we've had a lot of strain.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You already told us about the resistance of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, just before you move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's only a couple of days, the end of last week probably, that we actually had been in court as long as we had been out of court for the immediately preceding period. Everyone in this trial has worked under the same conditions and you've had longer than everyone else to deal with your issues. So it's becoming tiresome to hear every submission in writing or orally that you make preceded by a reference to the conditions under which you are working. Please concentrate on the work and spend your time on that rather than complaining.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we have been --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour's making representations on the record that I have to address then. Your Honour's raising these issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I am not raising an issue that you need to respond to. Move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: How were the relations and interactions between members of your company towards civilians during the course of the operation to liberate Orahovac?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: The relations between my members -- members of my company and other units participating in deblocking Orahovac and civilians were quite good. All of us acted in accordance with the law. Given that previously we were warned several times by senior officers, specifically my company commander, to strictly abide by the rules on warfare in relation to civilians. I can tell you that the relations with civilians were excellent and at a very good -- on a very good level.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you encounter fire upon your company, the PJP, from the side of the KLA or the armed opponents?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Fire was opened from the area known as Vran Stena as well as Mala and Velika Krasta. Orahovac lies in a valley, that's the configuration of the terrain, it's surrounded by hills. So they could open fire, and then once they withdrew from the town they had the dominant position so they could fire at us both with snipers as well as heavier weaponry. And later we established that they had this heavier weaponry entrenched in the place called Vran Stena and Mala Krasta, and those were new 12.7-millimetre Brownings.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Focusing for the moment still at 1998, can you tell us about any other places where you were engaged in activities against terrorism?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that was in several locations. Solely in places where we had received information that there were strong terrorist forces entrenched there and active in that area, where they put at risk security of all citizens of Kosovo and also posed a danger to security forces, meaning both police and the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you recall any specific locations where you were so engaged?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we were engaged in a place called Rakovina in order to deblock the road which under -- in that time was under the control of Siptar terrorists and where the safety of traffic wasn't good. So it was difficult for residents to move on the road in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: One correction for the record. I earlier mentioned Exhibit 6D761 and 6D237. 761 is a -- that's at page 58, lines 9 through 10 of the transcript. 761 is a duplication of 237. 237 is the only -- is the document, relevant document that is of record in these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I could ask you, did you participate in any actions in the Bajgora region in 1998 as part of your PJP company?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: I claim with full responsibility that I did not take part in any actions in Bajgora and I don't know to this day where that, I suppose it's a mountain, is located.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, in the course of -- strike that. You've already told us how your company commander instructed you to act properly towards civilians. Did you at any time in 1998 or 1999 receive orders to act improperly towards civilians, to commit crimes against civilians?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: That's not how it was. No instructions or orders came to us from our company commander. I claim with full responsibility that we were explicitly ordered under penalty to strictly abide by the Geneva Conventions as well as other legislation that pertains to wartime. So we received no orders whatsoever from our superiors in relation to any crime that we were allegedly supposed to commit.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me specifically with respect to 1998 or 1999 with respect to the hand-held radio communications in the course of activities, did you have occasion to use code words; and if so, what form did those code words take?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: Every company, or rather, company commander and deputy commander, commanders of platoons and commanders of squads had hand-held radio stations which they used for their communication, to communicate with each other. I was just an ordinary member of a reconnaissance squad and I did not have a radio with me; rather, the commander of my squad had it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In the course of 1998 and 1999, in the course of your fulfilment of your duties as a member of the PJP, and in the course of activities out in the field, did you ever hear of the use of such code words as "sibice," Serbian word for match; or "gumica," the Serbian word for eraser; or "obelezje," the Serbian word for mark?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't hear such terms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did you hear any code words?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I heard when I was in the vicinity of my squad commander who had a radio and who communicated with his company commander, it was only then that I heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Was it only his code word you heard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And what was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please repeat, who do you have in mind, squad commander or company commander?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So there were several you heard, several different commanders' code words were heard by you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You know what? Company commander had a code-name within our company. Since our company had five platoons, each platoon had its own commander, "komandir," platoon commander who had his own code-name. And within a platoon there were three squads with squad commanders, "komandir," who also had hand-held radio stations and they also had call-signs. And I can give you some examples if you want.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you -- did you in -- at any point in 1998 or 1999 eye-witness any crimes against civilians undertaken by members of your PJP company?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: I claim with full responsibility that I did not eye-witness a single crime nor were there any crimes when I was a member of that unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did -- strike that. How were you instructed by your superiors to react in situations where KLA were mixed with civilians?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: We had such situations very frequently on the ground that a group of Siptar terrorists was active from an area, and upon noticing that they could not put up resistance to our unit, given that we had better equipment and were better trained in tactics, they would desert their positions, discard their weapons as well as parts of uniforms, and mingle -- intermingle with columns of civilians who were there. As to an order from company commander or platoon commander or squad commander, we would always be warned not to open fire on such people because in a column of refugees there were innocent men, women, and children, and the elderly. And we were strictly forbidden to use any sort of weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, you identified -- you identified parts of uniforms that these KLA would discard. Could you describe what types of uniforms you saw the KLA to possess?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: We came across discarded parts of uniform, mostly top parts of uniforms, shirts, camouflage uniforms with green and red colours. I heard that those were mostly Chinese manufacture uniforms. And sometimes we would come across a better-quality camouflage uniforms with red and yellow dots on them, and later on I learned that those were German-make uniforms that they had discarded.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You indicated that they would discard their weapons. Did you have occasion to capture such discarded weapons after the activities of the KLA; and if so, what types of weapons were these and what actions were undertaken with respect to these weapons once they were collected?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: Our procedure was as follows. When our company was active we would frequently come across discarded weapons such as semi-automatic rifle with a wooden butt and also a machine-gun of Chinese make. We would also frequently come across pieces of heavy weaponry, 12.7-millimetre Browning. When encountering such weapons, given that we scouts would frequently go out on reconnaissance mission and after we certified that the area was safe so that others and other units could pass through it, we would inform the platoon commander. That is to say my squad commander would inform the platoon commander because that was the hierarchy chain of command, and then platoon commander would in turn inform the company commander who had a different line of communication with detachment commander. Usually those weapons would be assembled in one location, and if the terrain was such that it was easily accessible then weapons would be loaded onto a vehicle and then turned over to the command in some larger towns, such as Djakovica or Prizren.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, can you find a suitable time to interrupt?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Since I'm about to move to another topic, we should probably do it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Just before we break, you asked us to try to deal without undue formality with the substitute translation for 6D1004. There is no objection to that, and we will therefore authorise substitution of the new translation for the old. Mr. Milenkovic, we need to break at this stage; that will be for an hour. Could you please now leave the courtroom with the usher and we will see you again at 1.45.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.46 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milenkovic, I'd like to touch at first on an area that we did previously embark upon. You were talking about code-names and you indicated some of the various commanders within the -- within your company, et cetera. Could you tell us who was the commander of your reconnaissance squad? In Serbian I believe that would be "odeljenje."

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't understand the question sufficiently. Who was the commander of the reconnaissance squad? Was that your question? The commander of the reconnaissance squad was Mr. Zoran Markovic, called Cecko.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you recall what his radio code-name or call-sign was and the radio code-names or call-signs of any of the other commanders within the structure?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: His call-sign was Cegar 41/ -- 45/1, and the commander of the fourth squad was Cegar 45. The other commanders, and there were three of them, the commander of the reconnaissance squad had 45/1 as a call-sign; commander of the 2nd Armoured Mechanised Brigade [as interpreted] was 45/2; and the commander of the third squad had the call-sign Cegar 45/3.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now if we could focus on the time-period of 1999, and, sir, in 1999 did you and your company of the PJP have occasion to be in the village of Ljubizda near Prizren and could you describe the activities of yourself and the PJP relative to that assignment?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour, we have a transcript issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we have a problem with the transcript, as my colleague said, page 69, line 1, it says 2nd Armoured Mechanised Brigade, and this is not what the witness said. It's not a brigade, so we want to avoid confusion in the transcript and later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You gave the call-sign Cegar 45/2. Can you tell us whose call-sign that was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was the commander of the armoured mechanised squad as part of the 5th Platoon. It was a squad that moved around in an armoured truck, 110, that's what it was called, a truck that was armoured. It was protected by some metal items as well as rubber bands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, if we could focus for the time-period of 1999. In 1999 did you and your company of the PJP have occasion to be on assignment in the village of Ljubizda near Prizren and could you describe the activities of yourself and the PJP relative to that assignment?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. My company did have activities in the village of Ljubizda, it's a village close to Prizren. I cannot tell you exactly how many kilometres it's away from Prizren, but I think it's maybe up to 10 kilometres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could you describe the activities that your company and the other PJP engaged in in Ljubizda in 1999 during this time-period?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: From what my platoon, or rather, squad commander informed me, and he in turn was informed by the platoon and the company commanders, I received information that there was a strong terrorist group stronghold in that village that was very much entrenched, that they were firing quite fiercely on the civilian population, also that there was sniper activities and there was a lot of fear in that village. After preparation my company went towards Ljubizda where we naturally by establishment, us from the reconnaissance squad went first. When we came to the centre of the village and before that, we did not -- we were not exposed to any KLA fire or fire from the terrorist group. We found out from the inhabitants that this was a village where there was a headquarters of the Prizren city military department and that the village was under the command of Colonel Tomislav Mitic, about whom I know that he's actually from the same area as myself and that we actually lived some 3 to 4 kilometres away from each other. I wanted to meet that man because I had heard that this man was in Prizren. We asked around and the inhabitants said where this staff of the military department was, and we came to the house where the staff headquarters was located. This is where Colonel Mitic met us, and that was where I met him for the first time because as I said before, I had heard of the colonel but I did not know him personally. We spoke there for a little bit and he told us that there were no Siptar terrorist activities in the village, that the village was very quiet, and that there were no problems. He also informed us that the neighbouring village, the village of Korisa that was maybe some 5 to 7 kilometres away from Ljubizda, was where these strong entrenched terrorist groups were located and who were using sniper rifles and rifles of larger calibre to fire at civilians and other structures in the village of Ljubizda. We stayed. I have to say this again. Before that, my company commander also came, Mr. Nenad Stojkovic, who also spoke with Mr. Mitic. I don't know and -- what Mr. Stojkovic talked about with the detachment commander, but in about two or three hours we left Ljubizda and went towards Korisa.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just to be clear that we've got the correct information in English. The KLA were firing at you or firing at Ljubizda from a range of 7 kilometres?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I think I said, from what I can remember, that Ljubizda was about 5 to 7 kilometres away from the place of Ljubizda and the Siptar terrorists from that place who were entrenched there, because that village is at the foot of a mountain, probably there were terrorists who were closer to the village of Ljubizda and that is from where they fired at the inhabitants of the village and the other structures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you not know where they were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you please repeat the question. Who do you mean when you say "where they were"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The terrorists.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, I didn't know, but I heard from the colonel that the terrorists were in the nearby hills above the village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And how many of the civilian population had they killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And to clarify, how long in total were -- was your company the PJP in the village of Ljubizda?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot really tell you for sure, but I think it was four, five, possibly six hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And during that time-period did you have any other interactions with civilians apart from what you've already identified for us?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could you describe for me that contact.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: This was when we entered the village. I was able to see that in the village, and I even heard from Mr. Mitic, the population that was living there was divided or mixed, it was Serbian, Montenegrin, and Albanian. But I saw myself that when we entered the village people were disturbed or got agitated in a way, most probably from what I heard from them, they were afraid of the bombing of NATO aeroplanes and because of the activities of a large group of Siptar terrorists who were in the near -- immediate vicinity of the village and afraid of that, they were leaving their houses and going in a column that was right next to the village and then I really have no information about where they continued after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you have any information or knowledge of any of your superior officers issuing orders for civilians to be forcibly evicted from this village?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: Are you thinking of the village of Ljubizda?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't have that information. There was no such information. There was no order that people should be thrown out of the village, Albanians and so on. I responsibly state that we did not have such an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the village of Korisa. With respect to Korisa, did your company have occasion thereafter to go to Korisa?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you, and that question, you will be able to answer in a moment. Can I just be -- you've told us what orders you did not get. What were your orders when you went into the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I said that, in response to previous questions put to me by the Defence, that my company commander had information, I assume that he received it from the commander, that large terrorist groups of Albanian terrorists were in this village of Ljubizda who were entrenched and very well-armed and that they were firing at the civilian population that happened to be in the village and this is why --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Obviously when you arrive you see the situation for yourself. So what were the orders you had when you went into the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We couldn't see -- couldn't see if there were these strong terrorist groups in the village, but when we entered the village we received information from Mr. Mitic, whom I mentioned before, that there was no terrorist group activity in the village and that these groups were acting from the neighbouring village, from encampments that were closer to Korisa.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the question Mr. Ivetic asked you was: Did you go to Korisa? Can you answer that now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: With respect to Korisa, can you tell us of any activities in that village undertaken at that time by your company of the PJP?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: Moving from Ljubizda towards Korisa, the terrorists noticed our movement and they were withdrawing systematically towards the mountain above Suva Reka, so that when we entered the entrance to the village there were practically no inhabitants left in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And do you have any knowledge or information or did you ever hear of any order issued by commandant Mitrovic or any other PJP officer with respect to Korisa, encouraging -- encouraging theft in Korisa?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: This is not correct. I didn't receive any command from my platoon commander or squad commander who had a hand-held radio who was connected with the company commander. Since I was quite often close to the company commander and he was often there immediately in our vicinity, we were able to hear the commands being issued by the commander. So I did not hear such an order. There was no order like that, any kind of theft or any kind of crime that was counter to the Geneva Conventions or any other laws, all acts in violation of these laws were strictly forbidden.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Just waiting for the transcript and translation to catch up with you, sir. Now, sir, I'd like to move to another area of questioning and to try and do this in a very open way I would ask for Exhibit P2629 to be pulled up on e-court. Sir, have you had occasion to be shown this photograph and other photographs in this series previously?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am familiar with these photographs. They were shown to me at the district prosecutor's office for war crimes in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And when were those photographs shown to you and under what circumstances?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could you ask that again, Mr. Ivetic, since there was an overlap.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us when these photographs were shown to you in the district prosecutor's office for war crimes in Belgrade and under what circumstances?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: These photographs were shown to me, if I remember correctly, on the 5th of March, 19 -- 2007 at the war crimes section in Belgrade. Besides this photograph, I was shown four more --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I interrupt for just a moment. Mr. Ivetic, these appear to be under seal. I don't know why. Can anyone alert us to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, they were I think initially shown in connection with a protected witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So on their own, there is no problem?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, on their own I don't think there's a problem as long as we're not making a connection between him and that particular protected witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I believe these are the same pictures that were published in the newspaper article that the Prosecution and I had discussed earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll -- we'll lift the confidentiality from the photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, first of all, sir, are you depicted in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And could you -- could you -- I see that you were in the middle of answering the circumstances under which you were shown these photographs and then we had the discussion about the confidentiality of the photographs. Could you please finish your discussion about the circumstances surrounding when and how this photograph and if any other photographs were shown to you by the public prosecutor in Belgrade in March of 2007.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: In March, or rather, on the 5th of March, 2007, I was summoned to report to the UPOBOK in Belgrade in order to talk about the circumstances when these photographs were taken and about crimes that had taken place in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And do you happen to know or were you informed by the public prosecutor how these photographs had come to their attention?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I was informed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And what were the -- well --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't believe that we're treading on any issue of identifying anyone, but for the sake of caution perhaps we could just pop into private session to make sure that the question I asked does not lead to any production of any -- anything. I'm at Your Honour's discretion, actually. I was going to ask where -- what he was told about the photographs coming into the attention of the prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I don't know what the answer will be, but it could possibly raise an issue so I would join in that request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. We shall go into private session briefly. 16 [Private session]. [Confidentiality lifted by later order of the Chamber]

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in private session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could you now, sir, please tell us how -- what the prosecutor of the Belgrade district court told you with respect to how -- where these photographs had come from or your knowledge of the same?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: I received information from the prosecutor at the war crimes sector that the pictures came or the photos came from a colleague who was together in the company with me and who is from my area where I come from, and that he had given the photographs to Ms. Natasa Kandic, who published those pictures in the Danas newspaper, and this is what got them interested in the case. He didn't tell me actually the name of the person who provided the pictures.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, that part satisfies my question. If we could go back to open session, I think that we could deal with the rest in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Any reason why that should remain private, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, I don't think so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. The part recently heard in private session will be made public. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milenkovic, could you, please, in as much detail as possible explain for us the factual circumstances that led to the time in 1999 when this picture was taken. What had transpired prior to this picture being taken on the ground at this time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot remember the exact date when this happened, since this was a long time ago. The company commander informed us that larger groups of terrorists were to be found in the area of the locality of Vinogradi above I think it was the village of Randobrava, but please don't hold me to that. I'm not 100 per cent sure. I'm partially sure that it was above the Randobrava village. And then pursuant to the order for us to prepare in terms of what we needed to take with us of the equipment, we assumed that this was going to be a slightly larger action where we were supposed to free the road in that area of the territory that I mentioned earlier. We set off on foot, and I'm not quite sure here either but I think it's some 7 to 8 kilometres and there was a small wood where we, being tired from the long trip and the equipment that we were carrying and being tired from our previous stay in several places where these events were happening, we received an order from the company commander to stop for a while and to rest there. There was an armoured vehicle with us from my personal company that was armoured and where different things were that were essential for us, and I'm thinking here of food, water, ammunition, and some other items that were essential to us. While we were resting one of the members, since in that part of the cleansing there were other companies of the 37th Detachment taking part, thinking of the companies from Pirot, Prokuplje, Krusevac, probably, Vranje. One of the members of the Pirot company needed to go to the toilet, and he went some 15 or 20 metres in front of us in order to relieve himself. 10 to 20 minutes [as interpreted] later the man came running with his trousers down at his knees and shouted out to everyone: "Boys, I noticed a large group of terrorists, they have a large fortified position. Take up positions quickly. They're going to kill us." We took this very seriously. The company commander confirmed this and ordered that we take up positions and make ourselves as safe as possible to save our own lives. As we were moving and taking up the safest possible positions, the best-covered ones in the location, we must have been noticed by the terrorists who were at an elevation 400 to 500 metres away from us. As soon as they saw us, they opened extremely strong fire at my unit and the other units.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Why don't you just hold there for a second, I see my colleague's on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry, line 6, page 80, the witness said 10 to 20 seconds later, not minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if I can --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I can ask you, Mr. Milenkovic, what happened after fire was opened up on you and how long did that fire engagement last?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: That's what I was about to say. They opened extremely strong fire with automatic rifles and heavy machine-guns. The fighting lasted for about two hours. My company commander Mr. Nenad Stojkovic, since we were very close, informed the commander that we were under heavy fire, the Siptar terrorists had left their trenches -- in fact, they were firing from their trenches from a position dominant over us and they could easily take advantage of the situation and inflict losses. When he informed Commander Mitrovic, he also asked for assistance, meaning from the mortar squad. After about 10 minutes we received the support of mortars, but since we were not able to communicate with them, as the mortar squad was part of the 5th Platoon and was below the location of this event, we could not inform the commander of the mortar squad about anything and we could not guide him to the targets. However, those men who were trained for mortars did their job well and mortar shells landed in the heart of their trenches. The fighting lasted for about two hours -- I'm sorry, I forgot to mention that while the fighting was going on the company commander communicated very frequently with the commander because the commander wanted to know about the situation, he wanted to be kept posted, and he regularly issued orders to the commander of mine and other companies to be as careful as possible and to avoid losses and save the men. After two hours, my commander informed the commander of the detachment, Mr. Mitrovic, that fire had stopped and we were able to see without any visual aids, with the naked eye, we could see the terrorists running to the vineyards nearby. I heard distinctly that Commander Mitrovic ordered Nenad Stojkovic on the radio to evaluate the situation himself, and if it was possible to safely send the reconnaissance squad to do some scouting and see what really happened at the position from which the terrorists fired at us, to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And did you as part of the reconnaissance squad have occasion to advance or move into the position where the trenches of the KLA had been?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: No. We, the scouts, the six of us, took cover a safe position from which we fired as best we could at the position of the terrorists where they were firing from. The whole time that the fighting lasted, nobody among us made any attempt to go forward and reach them because their weaponry was very heavy and they could easily reach us and inflict heavy losses, which we wanted to avoid of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could you lead us to the point in time what transpired leading up to the picture and then after this picture was taken?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: I said that a moment ago. When Mitrovic informed Stojkovic, Stojkovic ordered the commander of the reconnaissance squad to go to the position from which the terrorists had fired. Since there was still some sporadic fire, we crawled and we managed with great difficulty, since we were under fire all the way, we managed to reach the trenches where the Siptar terrorists had fortified themselves. When we reached the point of destination, we took up the combat posture that we had learned well during training. We were well fanned out, 7 to 10 metres between each two of us. When we reached the trenches, we saw a horrific sight, several of them dead, blankets, ammunition, equipment scattered about, four or five Chinese-made machine-guns, if I remember correctly. And I recognised them easily because of -- because I had seen those Chinese machine-guns earlier when we seized them and turned them over to our commanding officers who drove them to their SUPs. We were very careful observing all the time, trying to make sure that nobody was watching us hidden in the vineyards from a position from which they could kill us. I heard our squad commander inform the company commander that we had performed our assignment, that the site was horrific, and the order he received then was to search the terrain very thoroughly and report back. We combed the terrain crawling, trying to avoid being seen from the terrorists hiding in the vineyards, trying to avoid getting killed. And at one point we heard somebody moaning from inside a connecting trench. As far as I can remember Dejan Mihajlovic, one of the scouts, and Zoran, the commander of the reconnaissance squad, were the first to go in. I was not far from there, and I heard from them that there were people wounded inside. I came out from behind a bush holding my rifle in the combat posture that I learned during training, and that's the posture you can see on the photograph as I'm standing over this seriously wounded man who was gasping for breath and there came a wheezing sound from his throat, he was so badly wounded. Nearby there was another wounded person. His wound was in the arm, in his thigh, and there was blood all over his head, but I'm not sure whether that was a shrapnel wound or there was just some staining from other wounds. In another photograph you would see a different picture. The commander --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a moment, Mr. Milenkovic. There's a part that the interpreter did not pick up. You started off by saying: "In another photograph there's a different picture ..." Could you continue from there, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I meant those photographs that the judge from the war crimes chamber showed me in Belgrade. I'm sorry. When Mr. Markovic, our commander, took that little bag from the man's shoulder, we thought it was one of their commanding officers, he opened the bag and found inside a telephone that we later realized was a satellite phone. He took the telephone and gave it to Goran Velickovic, deputy squad commander, who was also on this reconnaissance mission with us. Searching on through that bag, Zoran found a red notebook and a ball-point pen -- in fact, several pens. When he opened the notebook he found many entries. On one of the pages there was a list of persons, but I have to tell you that everything written there was in Albanian and none of us could read or understand Albanian. So we didn't know what it was. But when we came to one page we found perhaps 70 or so names from Orahovac, and I remember that distinctly because it wasn't the Serbian version Orahovac, it was in Albanian, Rahovec, and that's what told us that these persons listed were from Orahovac, Velika Hoca, Opterusa, and some other nearby villages. I can't remember all of them. Zoran was leafing through that notebook. The person whom you see in the photograph was still breathing wheezingly, he was so badly wounded. The commander of our squad took his portable radio, informed the company commander Stojkovic about the situation and the wounded people we'd found and what they were carrying. As we were doing that, another one of the scouts out there collected the weapons scattered around the trenches, and I believe there were three to four light machine-guns that were typically Chinese made with the round drum for ammunition. We put it all in one heap, and when our commander Zoran informed the company commander what we had found on the spot he probably told him to contact the detachment commander because he was the only one who was able to. And our Commander Zoran Markovic had another radio, providing direct link with the company commander; he must have received orders to give maximum care to these two wounded men and try to get them alive to the -- that truck, that armoured truck, 110, that we had left somewhere behind. I heard Zoran say to the company commander that one man was so badly wounded that he was about to die any minute. There was still sporadic firing going on. We were still afraid for our lives, and we had to execute that order and we tried to give them all the assistance we could, both medical and otherwise, because we knew we would need them alive for the sake of information they could provide us because one of them had what looked like a list of Serbs and other people from a nearby place who had been liquidated. We took some tent canvass and put on it, not this one who is in the photo but the other man who was carrying that little bag with documents. In addition to the bag, he also had a belt with a pistol, and on his jacket -- on top of his jacket he had a vest and in the vest there were stock ammunition clips for an automatic rifle, which indeed we found lying next to him. The person, the one who's in the picture, I noticed that he must have already received some assistance from one of his fellow fighting men. He had a tourniquet above his knee and his knee looked horrible. It was like a flower in bloom, which was an indication of a shrapnel wound, not a bullet. It must have been a mortar shell that hit him. The man was about to faint, to pass out, and you have to remember we were in danger ourselves. We put the other man on that piece of canvass and trying to run under cover taking turns, because there was six of us, we somehow managed to bring that wounded man to the truck where our company commander was waiting. The man whom we got to the truck was much less seriously wounded than the one we had left behind. He was able to speak Serbian. I think he said he hailed from Velika Krusa or Velika Hoca, I can't be sure now, and he asked for water. Since we were carrying a lot of equipment that was compulsory by regulation, there were very few of us carrying water and we must have used it up on the way there and very few of us had water. When we needed it for ourselves we would get some from our truck. So anyway, this man asked for water. I felt really horrible, I must say. He was a harrowing sight, he had a lot of blood on his head, he was bleeding from his arm and from his leg, and there was a puddle next to the truck from the rain that had fallen a few days earlier. We didn't have enough water in the truck so I took this clear water from the puddle, because it was really clear, in a plastic bag and brought it to the wounded man. He was unable to raise his arm because he was injured in the arm. He was just opening his mouth. I put the plastic bag close to his mouth, he tore it with his teeth and started to drink. Then Commander Nenad Stojkovic ordered us scouts to take up the circular defence position so as to make him safe because he had already informed the commander to send an investigation team. After this, we removed ourselves to 50 metres away and took up the circular defence position. Perhaps an hour or so later, maybe two hours, I can't be sure, one of us returned to the truck to get something, probably food because there was not much water there anyway, and night was already falling. I can't tell you now exactly which one of our scouts it was. And when he came back to us, he told us the wounded man had died. What happened later with him, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. At -- was your --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is that the one who's in the truck who died?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And the other one was left, the more seriously injured one was left where he was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that one, we tried to save him as well somehow, but since we were under heavy fire -- it was sporadic but still heavy --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic obviously wanted an awful lot of detail from you. I don't for my purposes at the moment. I just want to be clear. The one that we see in the photograph, he was the one left behind; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When we tried to help him and he was so badly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes or no. He know how badly -- is he the one who was left behind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, he was left there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Did he die?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did any --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: Just one -- if I may just add, Your Honours. That other one, I didn't see him die there on the spot. I heard only the next day when the investigation team had arrived, the one that had tried to come even earlier; however, after nightfall it was not safe for that investigation team to set off from Randobrava and come to our position so the investigation took place only the next day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I only need answers very specific to the questions I ask, and please bear that in mind if I ask you any questions. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You mentioned in the course of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just one moment, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: One thing is perhaps not clear. The person we see in the photograph, were you present when he died?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: He was the one left behind, is it? Was he the one left behind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: And he was injured.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: With respect -- let me try and clear up the other issue first. Judge Bonomy asked you about this individual. The other individual, were you present when the other individual died either, physically present with him when he died?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: No. I said that on the orders of the company commander ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, you indicated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There's an incomplete answer there, Mr. Ivetic, now. You're recorded as saying -- and this problem is caused by you not just answering the question that you're asked. You said something about: "I said that on the orders of the company commander ..." What were you trying to say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You'll have to repeat the question, because Mr. Ivetic had asked me for an extensive description of this incident and I gave --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's some time ago. You were just asked a moment ago: "Were you present when the other individual died either, physically present with him when he died?" And you said: "No. I said that on the orders of the company commander ..." And then we have no more. What were you going to say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have repeated that earlier as well, perhaps a minute or two prior to that. When we brought that person to the truck and we turned him over to the company commander and other people around the truck, the company commander ordered us to organize a circular defence to put ourselves in, circular defence position, in order to protect both ourselves and the people who were there in the vicinity and we did that. And that was 50 to 70 or 80 metres away, roughly, from the site where the event took place and where this person was left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Were any of the members of your company trained to provide medical attention?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: There was a doctor in the logistics squad some 8 kilometres away from the site of the event, and I've mentioned that earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Were you able to establish direct radio-to-radio contact with the doctor?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: While I was standing by the truck, the company commander attempted to call Cegar 45/2 or /3, I'm not sure, which is the personal call-sign for the logistics squad where the doctor was. However, since we used only hand-held radios, we didn't have other ones, since all relay stations had been destroyed for radio communications and due to the terrain, the configuration was not accessible, Nenad Stojkovic did not manage to establish contact with that squad to ask for the doctor and them to come to assist them. However, he informed Mitrovic, who I guess was in the vicinity of Prizren where the frequency was good enough in order to establish communication and they also had better radio equipment than the one that was in possession of the company commander and squad commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, with respect to when these items were shown to you at the public prosecutor's in Belgrade, you indicated other photographs. What was done with those photographs by the prosecutor? Or -- what did you ask the prosecutor to do with those photographs?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: The prosecutor in Belgrade showed me I think five photographs. The first photograph that was shown to me is the one that we can see on the monitors right now. Then I asked the judge, given that he claimed that they were made on the same camera and same negative, that they were developed from the same negative, I asked them to put the pictures in the chronological order. I wanted to see the photograph that was taken first up to the fifth, and the prosecutor did that. In the first picture and the only one that we see now, you can see me coming out of the bush with my gun at the ready. And when I put this on my computer at home I could see that the barrel of the gun is not pointed at this person at all. My finger is also not on the trigger.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I can ask you, do any of the other photographs that were shown to you by Investigator Stankovic when put in chronological order show this individual shown in this picture after you had -- after you had left, that is to say Prosecutor Stankovic, I apologise, investigative judge or Prosecutor Stankovic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know his name. I've forgotten it. I was shown five photographs. Out of those I think that on four photographs you can see the person who is shown on the first photograph. There is nobody else other than him and me. When asked by the prosecutor, since I was allowed to put questions, I asked the prosecutor, since it says at the bottom there's a caption saying that this is photo documentation of a murder. I asked him on the second or third picture, or rather, when I was asked on the second or third picture, Does the person there look alive or not? I said -- the answer was, He looked alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now to your knowledge -- strike that. Since you gave this interview last year to the prosecutor, you have not been -- strike that. Have you been charged with any wrong-doing relating to this incident?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: To your knowledge, have any of the various individuals from your PJP company been charged by the prosecutor's office in Belgrade with criminal responsibility for the events -- for the events --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: I know very well that nobody was charged. You asked me but I didn't manage to complete my answer. I offered to the war crimes prosecutor who questioned me at the time to give me a test, a polygraph test so that I could prove I was telling the truth.
