Because I know for a fact that none of us killed that person. This person died as a result of serious wounds. You can see in the picture the state that his leg was in, and it is obvious that this wound didn't come from a gun or a small-calibre weapon -- from a rifle or a small-calibre weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milenkovic. I know this has been a trying ordeal for you. I thank you for your time and cooperation.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. Mr. Aleksic, no questions? Mr. Bakrac. Mr. Milenkovic, you'll now be cross-examined by the Prosecutor, Mr. Hannis. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Milenkovic, you told us that when you first were in the police you worked at the police station in Crna Trava and then in 1997 at your own request you were transferred. Why did you request a transfer in 1997?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: Since I was born in a lovely town called Lipovica, as I've told you, which is 8 kilometres from Vlasenica -- Vlasotince and since we built our family home and we wanted our children to go to good schools and we wanted general prosperity for our family, we wanted to move to Vlasotince because the place where we were living at the time didn't really offer any good prospects for me or for anybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Are you still a member of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Where is that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: Leskovac police administration, police branch office in Vlasotince.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And who is the current chief of the Leskovac police station? Or maybe I should say the Leskovac SUP.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: It's not SUP. Lieutenant-Colonel Slavoljub Sakic is chief of the Leskovac SUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And during your time with the MUP, have you ever been subject to disciplinary procedures?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, once or twice, something like that. Minor omissions in service. If necessary, I can give you details.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, please. Would you tell us about the first time, when was that and what was that for?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: The first time was -- it will probably be funny to you, but I didn't put a cap on my head and I had a commander who was quite strict so I was fined with a fine of 10 per cent of my salary. On the second occasion, either in 1989 or 1990, I think it was in 1990, I had a traffic accident in a police vehicle, and at the time it was established that there was an omission on the part of my commander and other colleagues and I was punished by assigning me to a different job and I suffered the consequences without going on a sick leave. I don't think that it was a major violation of my work duty. A traffic accident can happen to anyone in a company or a service vehicle too.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sure. And when approximately was the first time you got the discipline for failing to put the cap on your head, what year?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: That was long time ago. I think it was in 1986 or 1987. To tell you the truth, I have to give you another example that would explain that. At that time there was a celebration going on celebrating the day of youth and there was a -- something of a relay race --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Let me interrupt you --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: -- and I think up to my commander who was quite a strict person.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you there. Apart from those two occasions, are you saying those are the only two times during your career in the MUP that you were disciplined, right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You told us then that after that first transfer you had another request to be transferred and you went to the A formation for a company of the 37th Detachment. Why did you request that second transfer?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: I considered myself to be a stable person in physical and mental sense and that I was able to do that job. It was -- I was personally proud of being a member of the 37th Detachment. It wasn't a matter of money. And in that formation I had my old friends, both friends from school and from the police station where I worked, and this was the decisive factor in my decision to join the A formation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you have a nickname you were known by by your fellow PJP members?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What was that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: Sisarka.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And could you explain the difference to us between an A formation and a B formation in the 37th Detachment of the PJP or in PJP detachments. What's the difference between A and B?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: There is no particular difference, great difference, the main difference being that members of the 37th Detachment were mostly men who were psychologically ready, ready to carry out delicate, difficult, and complex assignments at any time, assignments given to us by the command. As I have said previously to your earlier question, we used that unit in order to capture and arrest serious criminals, to locate terrorist groups, and to maintain law and order in large competitions, football games, and in large gatherings.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I may have misunderstood some earlier evidence in this case. I understood that the A detachments were the ones that were manoeuvre units and went out and did things, and that the B detachments were territorial or perhaps reserve. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. You told us earlier today at page 51, line 12, that I think you were in the 4th Company of the 37th Detachment, which consisted of -- the 37th Detachment consisted of six companies, and you named the places they were from. Which -- where were the people in the 4th Company from, what geographic area?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: The 4th Company comprised members of the secretariat in Leskovac and other organizational units that belonged to the secretariat in Leskovac, such as police station in Crna Trava, Vlasotince, in Medvedja, in Lebane, in Bunik as well as two police squads which were part of the Leskovac and that was the one in Vucje and in --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch the last location.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you repeat the last location for us. The interpreter didn't hear that.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: In Vucje and in Pecenjarice.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: Which was part of the police station in Leskovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were there six companies of the 37th Detachment in both 1998 and in 1999 during the war?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know how many companies for sure there were in the 37th Detachment in 1999?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sure about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how many was that, was that six?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you told us about the pay difference between being a member of the PJP and being I guess just a general-duty policeman, and that doesn't sound like very much of an incentive to join the PJP. It's not for the money obviously, right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So what is the attraction? Do you get better uniforms?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: Are you referring to me specifically?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Or anybody joining the PJP. Do you have a better uniform than a regular policeman?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if he's asking about the witness, I have no objection; if he's asking for the witness to speculate about why other people join the PJP, I do have an objection, based on speculation and foundation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, my question now is just a generic question. Do the PJP have better uniforms than the regular policemen. Now, it may be an incentive for one guy and not another, but I'm right now just trying to establish if there's some quality difference in uniforms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. You can ask that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do I need to repeat the question, sir, or ...

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do the PJP have better-quality uniforms than regular policemen?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think that the quality of uniforms was significantly different. There were just minor nuances.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How about equipment? Is the PJP equipment better?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: At the outset I told you that according to the rules on weapons of police employees, at the time when I was a member of the 37th Detachment everybody received identical weapons and that was a CZ pistol and then automatic rifle 7.62-millimetres.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what kind of weapon would a regular policeman have?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your rifle --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. By your leave. May I?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: You asked me previously if I understood it well, or rather, would you please repeat your previous question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure how far back you want me to go. I asked you about what kind of a weapon a regular policeman would have. Do you mean the one before that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. What weapons does a regular policeman have. A regular policeman performing regular duties within his police station would be issued a CZ-99 pistol without an automatic rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And what brand or make was your automatic rifle?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: My automatic rifle was a so-called Kalashnikov 7.62-millimetres, M-62.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What kind of stock does that have? Is the stock made out of plastic or wood or what?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: It's made out of metal, the butt is made out of metal.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you get any kind of per diem or combat pay when you were sent to Kosovo over and above the usual salary?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How much was that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to say what the amount was. I'm not certain any longer. I can't answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, was it more significant than the pay difference between a PJP and a regular policeman, which you explained to us was a negligible amount?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: I wish to inform you here that a salary was something we received for our regular tasks and duties. As for the compensation for going on special tasks, that's quite a different matter. Now, exactly what the amount was, I can't remember any longer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is rather different from my understanding of this situation. The extra that you got which you said was about -- instead of a hundred dinars a month it would be 110 dinars, was that only when you were actually on PJP assignment or did you get that extra all the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. This 0.42 per cent or 0.43 per cent quotient was something we received on the basis of the decision of the chief of the secretariat, and that lasted for as long as we were members of that detachment. Now, what the Prosecutor is asking about is some kind of a compensation that was paid pursuant to some rules that had been adopted at a higher level that I know nothing about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand that. Thank you. In fact, though, this 0.42 per cent that I found a very difficult figure to comprehend before, when you put it into real money it's 10 per cent of the salary. That may not be much, but that's what it seems to be in real money. Now we're talking about something different --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely so, and I told you that it wasn't about the money.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I quite understand that. Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Milenkovic, were you -- during your time in Kosovo in 1998 and 1999 were you aware of some Russian volunteers fighting with you and/or with the VJ in the Prizren area? Were you aware of such a unit?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: I state with full responsibility that in my company as well as in my detachment there were no volunteers, be it Russian or of any other nationality. I did hear stories that allegedly there were fighters, both on the side of the KLA and on our side; however, I didn't see them nor can I tell you that I came across any of the Russian volunteers anywhere else, least of all in our detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Did your detachment sometimes engage in joint activities with parts of the 549th Motorised Brigade under -- which was under Colonel Delic? You did, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: I have heard of that brigade. Now, whose brigade it was, under whose command, I have no idea. I was just an ordinary policeman carrying out orders of my squad commander, so I really wouldn't be able to answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'll come back to that. Let me show you a photo. This is Exhibit P1596. You were asked some questions about the PJP uniforms and about wearing ribbons during parts of 1998 and 1999. Can you see that photograph on your monitor now?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Based on those uniforms, can you tell us anything about what unit or what organization these men are associated with? Is that --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know these boys, but judging by their appearance and the way they're standing and the way they're dressed, not according to regulation, I believe they can't be regular members of the police and I don't know these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Are those not the blue camouflage police uniforms that were worn in 1998?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: Those are police uniforms, but the vests these people are wearing do not belong to police uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Isn't it true that in Kosovo in 1998 and in 1999 at times there were problems with shortages of uniforms and boots for both the MUP and the VJ?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Is that because in your detachment you never had any shortage or problem with uniforms or boots?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: That worked really well in our unit, in our company, because organization was at an enviable level in our company. If you allow me to continue, I would say that all of them -- may I?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: All those who were sent to perform assignments would be issued with uniforms that they kept at home, so they were always tidy and always ready to put on their uniform according to regulation. And we were all uniformly dressed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I don't know if you can tell from the photo on your monitor, but you see the two men lying on their side on the ground. The one on the right, can you tell us what's on that patch on his left sleeve? I don't know if we're able to use the magnifying tool to enlarge that portion of the photograph.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: If you could. I cannot make this out. I have 20/20 vision, but I still can't make this out. I cannot distinguish the inscription.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. You're familiar with police uniforms in Serbia in 1998 and 1999, right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And isn't -- wasn't there a similar patch in terms of the shape and colours that were worn on some police uniforms that said either "policija" or "milicija"?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: There may be some similarity, I can't see properly, but if you look at the left-most person on the picture, if you look at his trousers and the trousers of the one next to him, you will see they are not consistent with the colour of trousers that we were issued with. Ours were blue camouflage with distinct insignia of the police. Another remarkable thing is the boots worn by the left-most person. They are not of army colour. We had our own boots that were standard issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If you would take a look, you'll agree with me that these men are all wearing on their shoulders, on the left shoulder, a red ribbon and on the right shoulder a white ribbon; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we now look at Exhibit 6D667.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is a document we've seen before, not you, sir, but before you were here, which purports to be a plan for marking MUP and VJ units between 25 and 31 July 1998. You were in Kosovo during that time-period, right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: I have a problem with interpretation. I didn't understand you very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were you in Kosovo during the time of 25 to 31 July 1998?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And can you read this document where it says that this is a plan for marking MUP and VJ units during that time-period? You see that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you'll see that on the 26th of July the markings were red ribbon on the left shoulder and a white ribbon on the right shoulder. In your company in the 37th Detachment did you wear ribbons during July of 1998?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: We had ribbons, but they were yellow, blue, and red, and I believe they started to be worn -- I can't be 100 per cent sure, but I'm 90 per cent sure it was end April/early May. But it's more likely that the beginning was on the 24th or the 25th of April, if my memory serves me right. It was at that time that we started to wear ribbons precisely for that reason, and I remember one specific case when one colleague was kidnapped --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. You're going beyond my question at this point. So to your memory you wore blue ribbons and not -- and not white ribbons?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: Not white ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And no one's ever told you you've had problems distinguishing colours? You're not colour-blind, right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I'm not colour-blind.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You told us --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm a little confused here. He's talking about April. I believe earlier he testified April -- I'm not listening to the translation so I don't see that the -- if counsel could ask what year we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you want to clarify that, Mr. Hannis? The end of April or early May which year?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, actually I was talking about July 1998 first and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, we know that, but is the witness talking about the same year?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's what I need to find out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Are you telling us that in July 1998 you wore blue, yellow, and red ribbons and you didn't wear any white ribbons in July of 1998?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: I can't tell you that. I really can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You mentioned --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, just before moving off. You were talking about this beginning on the 24th or 25th of April. Which year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1999 I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Earlier in your evidence you told us of ribbons being worn in 1998 and 1999.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really can't answer this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You told us about your problem with your facial skin in the beard. Did you get any kind of medical approval to not shave because of that condition so that you could show it to officers who might give you a hard time about having a beard?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: The doctor informed my company commander himself. I even had a problem when he didn't let me go home for the weekend because I had such a long beard, I was so disciplined, and even the doctor late Branislav Bane asked my company commander to let me not shave for ten days or so at least. But I myself couldn't stand it anymore. There were no proper conditions there to keep clean and I had to shave it off because I was bothered by it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could you tell us approximately when you were first sent to Kosovo in 1998?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: I think sometime in April.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When you were preparing to testify here didn't anything about that refresh your memory about when you first came to Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's the kind of information that would be contained in your personnel file, right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand this question. Can you repeat?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Wouldn't that kind of information be reflected in your personnel file, the date that you first were sent to Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILENKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Every member of the PJP had a special -- his own entry in the register, so there is precise information when I was sent to Kosovo, it's just that I don't have it at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, this would be an appropriate point for me if it's convenient to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis. Mr. Milenkovic, we have to complete our hearing for the day at this stage and resume tomorrow; that means that you will require to return to complete your evidence tomorrow, and that will be at 9.00 in this courtroom. Meanwhile, it is an important rule that you must have no communication with anyone at all about any aspect of evidence in this case. You can communicate about anything else, but absolutely off limits is any communication about the evidence. Now could you please leave the courtroom with the usher and we will see you again tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.
